title: How to Choose the Right Crate Size for Your Puppy
description: A crate that fits today, still works in six months, and stays clean enough to be her safe place. Here is how to get there.

quick: For most puppies, choose a crate where she can stand up, turn around and lie down stretched out. Use a divider panel to make the space smaller while she is little, then move it back as she grows. Too much room can lead to one corner becoming a toilet, so check her size and comfort every few weeks.

faq.q: What size crate for a puppy should I buy if I don't know her adult size?
faq.a: Start with what you can see now, and ask your breeder, rescue or vet for an estimate of adult size. If you truly can't tell, choose a crate sized for the adult dog you expect and use a divider to shrink the space for the early months. Mixed breeds are harder to predict, so plan to adjust as she grows and keep an eye on her comfort.

faq.q: Can I use a crate divider for my puppy?
faq.a: Yes, and most families find it easy. A divider panel lets you make the crate small enough that she can stand, turn and lie down, but not so big that she can use one corner as a toilet. Move the divider back as she grows, and check that she still has room to lie down comfortably. Remove it once she is fully grown or clearly has more room than she needs.

faq.q: Is a crate too big for a puppy?
faq.a: It can be. If there is a bed at one end and an empty floor at the other, a puppy may keep the sleeping end clean and use the far corner instead. That isn't stubbornness. The space is simply bigger than she needs. Shrink it with a divider, take her out often, and reward her when she goes in the right place.

faq.q: How do I know if my puppy's crate is the right size?
faq.a: Watch her. She should be able to stand without her head touching the top, turn around without bumping the sides, and lie down on her side with her legs mostly stretched out. If she is pressed against the walls or can't get comfortable, she needs more room. If she is using a corner as a bathroom, she probably has too much.

faq.q: Should I buy a bigger crate so my puppy can grow into it?
faq.a: Many families buy a crate sized for the adult dog and then add a divider, and it works well for a lot of puppies. The trade-off is a few weeks of managing the space. The upside is that you don't have to replace the crate every few months. Just keep checking her size and how she settles in it.

faq.q: Will a puppy sleep better in a smaller crate?
faq.a: Some puppies feel more secure in a snug space, because there is less room to wander around while they are half asleep. Snug is not the same as cramped, though. Your puppy should always be able to lie down and stretch comfortably. Every puppy is different, so pay attention to how she settles at bedtime and how she wakes up.

html:
It is 2am. Your eight-week-old puppy has just wriggled out of the blanket you tucked around her, and you are standing in the hallway looking at a crate that the box says fits a medium dog. Too big? Too small? Nobody told you this part. If you have been wondering what size crate for a puppy actually makes sense, you are in the right place. The best crate size for a puppy is one where she can stand up, turn around and lie down stretched out, with a little room to spare but not so much that one corner becomes a toilet.

Here is the honest bit. Every puppy is different, and breed, weight and temperament all change what works. Still, the approach below holds for most first-time homes. Measure your puppy as she is now, plan for the size she will be as an adult, and use a divider to keep the space snug while she is small. You can do all of that without buying a new crate every month.

Measure the room your puppy actually needs

Forget the number on the box for a minute. Get out a soft tape measure and check your puppy at her current size. Measure her length from the tip of her nose to the base of her tail, her height from the floor to the top of her head while she stands, and the width across her shoulders. Write them down, because you will be comparing them to the crate's inside dimensions, which are not always listed clearly.

Then try the three tests that matter more than any measurement. Can she stand up without ducking her head? Can she turn in a full circle without bumping the sides? Can she lie down on her side with her legs mostly stretched out? If the answer is yes to all three, the crate fits her now. If she has to curl up to sleep, she needs more room. Watch her for a day or two, because puppies often sleep in odd positions and you will learn more from what she does than from what you planned.

Why you plan for the adult dog

Puppies grow faster than most people expect. A crate sized perfectly for the puppy you brought home may be outgrown in a few months, and that means buying a second crate, moving her bedding and getting her used to a new space all over again. Many families find it easier to start with a crate sized for the adult dog and manage the extra room with a divider.

The catch is that nobody can predict adult size with certainty. A photo of her parents helps a little, and mixed breeds are especially hard to guess. Ask your breeder, rescue group or vet for an estimate, and remember that growth varies from one puppy to the next. If you are not sure, plan for a bigger dog and be ready to adjust the divider as you go.

Use a divider to keep the space small

Most crates sold for puppies come with a divider panel, and if yours does not, a sturdy divider can often be added separately. The idea is simple. You shrink the crate to the size your puppy needs right now, and you move the wall back as she grows. It keeps her safe and comfortable without giving her a corner to ignore.

Setting up the divider step by step

  1. Put the divider in the closest position that still lets your puppy stand, turn and lie down. Check it with the three tests above.
  2. Add a bed or soft blanket on her side of the divider, and keep the other side clear of bedding.
  3. Watch her for a few days. If she is cramped, wakes up stiff, or can't turn around, move the divider back a notch.
  4. When she starts to stretch out with plenty of room, or when she is using the empty side for a toilet, it is time to open the crate a little more.
  5. Remove the divider when she is fully grown or clearly has more room than she needs, and keep checking her comfort after each change.

Expect to adjust the divider several times in the first months. That is normal. It is much easier to move a panel than to buy a new crate.

When a crate is too big

The first time a puppy has more room than she needs, many of them choose a corner and use it as a bathroom. It is one of the most common surprises for new owners, and it can feel like a setback, even when the puppy is doing exactly what puppies do. If she has a bed at one end and a big empty floor at the other, she may keep the sleeping area clean and go in the far corner instead.

If you notice this, don't scold her or rub her nose in it. That only makes the crate feel less safe. Instead, shrink the space with the divider, take her outside more often, especially after naps, meals and play, and praise her warmly when she goes where you want. Our potty schedule by age walks through timing in more detail, and it pairs well with a snugger crate.

Crate sizes as your puppy grows

Age gives you a rough guide, but her body is the better measure. Use the table below as a starting point, then check her comfort every week or two.

Age What to check Divider setting
8 to 10 weeks Can she stand, turn and lie down with no spare room for a toilet? As close as possible to her size
10 to 12 weeks Is she cramped, or is she sleeping with her legs stretched out? Move back a notch if she is squashed
3 to 4 months Is she sleeping at one end and using the other for a toilet? Open a little more as she grows
4 to 6 months Is she close to adult height and length, and comfortable in the full space? Often fully open, or removed

8 to 10 weeks

This is the tightest stage. Your puppy is small, sleepy and still learning that the crate is a good place. Keep the divider close and the bedding simple. A soft blanket is often enough, and it is easier to clean if she has an accident. Expect some crying in the first nights, which is normal, and our article on puppy crying at night explains what is usually going on.

10 to 12 weeks

Puppies can grow quickly at this stage, and what fit last week may feel snug now. Recheck the three tests and move the divider back if she needs it. Many owners are surprised by how fast this changes, so a weekly check is worth the thirty seconds it takes.

3 to 4 months

By now, most puppies can hold their bladder for longer stretches and are more likely to use the crate as a bed rather than a space they are trying to keep clean. This is a good time to open the divider a little, but watch for signs of too much room, like a corner that smells or a bed pushed to one side.

4 to 6 months

Your puppy is getting close to her adult size, although some dogs keep filling out for longer. Check her length, height and comfort again. Many families remove the divider at this point, and some keep the crate in a fixed size for the rest of the dog's life. Use your own observations here, because every puppy finishes growing on her own schedule.

Choosing a crate you can actually live with

Once you know the size you need, pick a crate that you will be happy to use every day. Look for a door big enough for her to walk through easily, latches that feel secure, and a floor tray that slides out for cleaning. A crate that is hard to clean is harder to keep fresh, and you will be cleaning it more often than you expect in the early weeks. Whichever crate you choose, make sure it has a divider or the option to add one.

It also helps to think about the whole first-week setup. Our new puppy checklist covers the crate alongside bowls, bedding, and the other basics, so you can buy things once instead of in a rush.

Before she is left alone in the crate, remove loose bedding she could pull apart and swallow, cords, and any toy with strings or small parts that could come loose.

Making the crate a place she likes

Size is only half the story. A crate that is the right size but feels scary will not work for long. Start with the door open, let her wander in and out, and toss a treat inside. Feed some meals in the crate, and stay nearby for the first few short stays so she can see you. Build up slowly, with the door closed for a minute, then five, then longer while you are in the room. Our guide to crate training a puppy covers this step by step, and every part of it relies on rewards, never on punishment or using the crate as a time-out.

If your puppy seems anxious in the crate, slow the process down rather than pushing through. Some puppies settle in a day and others take a couple of weeks. Both are normal, and you know your puppy better than any chart does.

When to ask a professional

Most crate questions are about fit and routine, and you can usually solve them at home. But some signs need a vet, not a new divider. Call your veterinarian if your puppy is straining to pass urine or stool, has blood in her urine, seems unusually thirsty, is wheezing or breathing hard, or stops eating. If she is limping, struggling to stand, or has trouble climbing in and out of the crate, get her checked before you change the setup. Growth concerns, such as a puppy who seems much bigger or smaller than expected for her age, are also worth a vet visit. A trainer or behaviourist can help with ongoing crate distress, especially if it lasts beyond the first few weeks.
